newsitem.title: USA: New issues dear, but competitives are costliest.
newsitem.headline: New issues dear, but competitives are costliest.

text.p: While new municipal bond issues have been coming rich to the secondary market for about a year, competitive offerings in particular have gotten so pricey that some buyers say they barely look at them.
"I just don't fool with them," Jan Terbrueggen, a vice president and portfolio manager at Nuveen Flagship, said, adding that new issues overall are "expensive."

"I see deals come that are like nine-times oversubscribed, and you look at it and say, 'I could do as well or maybe five basis points better in the secondary market,'" Terbrueggen said, adding that while a few recent new issues have been priced well, he couldn't name any off hand.
The secondary and primary market price gap is most apparent with competitive offerings as underwriters compete for business, the portfolio manager said.

"There are a lot of bankers out there that are looking for a reason for existing, and I think that's been a story for about a year," Terbrueggen said. "A lot of them are saying I can name that tune, I can price that bond at this level, and then they just pray the market bails them out or something."
Bewildering as it is, those costly competitive deals appear to be finding buyers, Terbrueggen said.
"It's not like we've got tons of cash to put to work," he said.
Tom Moles, a managing director at J&W Seligman, echoed many of Terbrueggen's sentiments.
"That's kind of the way we think too," Moles said.
While Moles occasionally sees an attractively priced issue, most of the time it is a negotiated deal, he said.

"I don't think we've done a competitive deal in six months," Moles said. "You maybe looking at two or three different scales, and you like those levels, and all of a sudden it comes in 20 basis points richer," he said.

While mutual funds used to dominate the market, property and casualty companies are back "in pretty good size," and retail investors have returned, despite the apparent slow down in mutual fund business, Moles said.

"So there is demand out there, especially in state-specific names," he said. "If you get a state specific that's got a high tax, a Maryland piece of paper, a Virginia or something like that, there's just a scramble for it."
A municipal analyst said while some may shun competitive issues, many buyers like them "because they are never criticized at a policy meeting."
Should the market turn south and a portfolio manager be questioned about a particular purchase, he or she can more easily defend a competitive offering by pointing to close bidding.
"If you bought it in the secondary, you may be questioned," he said."
